implementation_notes: Java's native form: every object has an intrinsic lock and a single wait set, so marking a method synchronized serialises it against the object's other synchronized methods and gives callers a happens-before edge; the API documentation calls this entity the monitor lock. Waiting requires ownership of the lock and Object.wait releases it atomically, so the guarded-block idiom (while (!predicate) wait();) is mandatory because a notification may not be the one the thread waited for. The intrinsic monitor has no timed or interruptible wait, no multiple wait sets and unspecified fairness, so where those are needed the same object is rebuilt from java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock and Condition.
pitfalls: wait/notify/notifyAll throw IllegalMonitorStateException unless the calling thread owns the object's monitor, and wait throws InterruptedException while clearing the interrupt status, so the caller must decide how to propagate it.
One wait queue per object makes notify() unreliable when several predicates are involved: use notifyAll plus a predicate loop, and accept the thundering herd.

Static synchronized methods lock the Class object, not the instance, so mixing them with instance synchronization silently serialises two different sets of callers; callbacks and I/O while holding the monitor cause nested monitor lockout.

variants.name: ReentrantLock + Condition (multiple wait sets, timed waits)
variants.implementation_notes: Condition factors the Object monitor methods out into distinct objects, so one monitor can have several wait sets - one condition per predicate - and signal() can wake exactly the waiters that the state change helps, instead of notifyAll over a single queue. The lock is explicit: lock()/unlock() in a try/finally, newCondition() to create the conditions, and await/awaitNanos/awaitUninterruptibly for the three waiting forms, with optional fairness. This is how java.util.concurrent's own bounded buffers are built and the standard escape hatch when the intrinsic monitor's missing timeouts, missing multiple wait sets or unspecified fairness matter.
pitfalls: The Condition must be created from the same lock that is used to await it, unlock() must be in a finally block, and a forgotten unlock turns the object into a permanent deadlock.

Condition.signal() wakes one waiter of that condition only; spurious wakeups remain permitted by the interface, so keep the predicate loop, and remember that fairness is off by default and starves writers under load.
Mixing a ReentrantLock with synchronized blocks on the same object creates two independent locks and defeats both.
